Lecture 06

GGPLOT

Q1

Biscoe island had the most count of penguins.

Without theme minimal we could still see the bar plot, however, it did make the plot look cleaner and removed the gray background. It also added light gridlines

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=island)) +
  geom_bar(fill="pink") +
  theme_minimal()

Q2

The general shape seems to be bimodial

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "lightpink") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="black"))

bins 30

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "lightpink") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="black"))

bin 60

  ggplot(penguins, aes(x=body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "lightpink") + 
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="black"))

Higher bin number makes the bars narrower and gives a more detailed representation of the data with smaller range of x values.

The mean for 3 different islands is definitely different. Gentoo has the highest mean and Adelie has the lowest mean. Gentoo’s range was about (4500 - 6500) while adelie was(2500-4000) and Chinstrap was in middle (3000-5000)

BOXPLOTS

Q3

part 1

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=species, y=flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "pink") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="azure1"))

Gentoo have longest flippers in average. They seem to be around 210-215mm.

part 2

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=body_mass_g, y=sex, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="azure1"))

Male and female species do differ in mass, female species seem to be in lower mass range than the male ones. Adding fill=species does help with readability, it colors the inside of shapes based on the species category.

Scatterplots

Q4

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=bill_length_mm, y=bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="azure1"))

The relation between bill_depth_mm and bill_length_mm seems to be positive, since as bill length increases bill depth seems to slightly increase (in general)

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=bill_length_mm, y=bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect())

Yes, changing the points by species helps make the species bill length and depth clearer. Each species forms its own group and the negative relation is more obvious.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=bill_length_mm, y=bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill="azure1"))
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

The line doesn’t fit the data perfectly but it does showcase the negative relation.

#Faceted scatter plots ## Q5

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y=body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

I would say gentoo seems to have the strongest relationship.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y=body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(sex~species) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

For all the species there seems to be a positive relation between body mass and flipper length. Adding facet_grid also seperates the species by sex.

Create a complex figure

Q6

ggplot(penguins, aes(x=flipper_length_mm, y=bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

REFLECTION

The most fun part for me was toggling with the colors to make it look cuter, Dr Samuk taught me how to change the background color. Other than that it was also fun to observe the different graphs and the most confusing part was facet i’m skill kind of confused on difference between facet wrap and facet grid

Q7

penguins_messy <- penguins_messy %>%
  mutate(
    bill_mm = as.numeric(
      str_replace_all(notes, "(.*bill=)|mm", "")
    )
  )
## Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.

##   ""))`.
## Caused by warning:
## ! NAs introduced by coercion

Reflection:

The most interesting part of the exercise was using regular expressions to pull numbers out of messy text and the hardest part was understanding what the symbols in the regex meant, especially things like .*, |, and parentheses. It’s not very intuitive at first, and it’s easy to remove too much or too little text if the pattern is slightly wrong.#

Question 2

  bind_rows(slice_sample(penguins_clean, n = 30, replace = TRUE))

penguins_dup %>%

number of rows after removing duplicates is 333 duplicates can mess up data analysis by inflating sample sizes which could lead to skewed statistics..

Using across is better, as it is more time efficient and convenient.You can also reuse the same pattern to try multiple different codes.

      bill_length_mm < 40 ~ "short",

      bill_length_mm >= 50 ~ "long"
    )

Q7

instrument_meta <- tibble(
  instrument_id = c("caliper_A", "caliper_B", "caliper_C"),
  calibration_mm = c(0.2, 0.5, 1.0),
  manufacturer = c("Mitutoyo", "Fowler", "Generic")
)

penguins_instrumented <- penguins_clean %>%
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) %>%
  mutate(
    instrument_id = case_when(
      year == 2007 ~ "caliper_A",
      year == 2008 ~ "caliper_B",
      year == 2009 ~ "caliper_C"
    )
  ) %>%
  left_join(instrument_meta, by = "instrument_id")

ncol(penguins_instrumented)
## [1] 11
ncol(penguins_clean)
## [1] 8

Number of Columns in penguins_instrumented is 11 and penguins_clean is 8

Reflection

Using across and select() was the most fun part for me since I realize that I didn’t have to type in every column name, and it made coding way easier. Most confusing for me was figuring out the regex expressions.

This is definitely going to be useful later since grouping could be useful in various data analysis based works, specially if you are getting into reserch or genetics.
